analysis.one_liner: Lets states limit how long freight trains can block road crossings.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, federal law generally overrides state rules that would limit how long a train can sit across a road crossing, so towns cannot enforce their own limits. This bill would change federal law so states could set time limits on blocked crossings. It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: Motorists, bicyclists, and pedestrians who get stuck at crossings; emergency responders such as ambulances and fire trucks that lose minutes or reroute when a crossing is blocked; and the towns that would regain the power to enforce their own crossing rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, emergency responders, and towns near crossings

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends federal railroad law so that it 'does not preempt a State' from adopting limits on how long a railroad may block a highway-rail crossing [S3].

The CRS summary explains why this matters: courts have generally found state laws on obstructed crossings preempted by federal law, rendering them unenforceable, and this bill would remove that preemption for crossing-blockage limits [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Freight railroads, which would face new state-by-state limits on how long trains can block crossings, with added operating costs and potential network delays where limits are strict. Any added freight-rail cost is typically passed into shipping prices, which touches businesses and consumers only indirectly.

drawbacks.text: Railroads and federal courts have long treated crossing rules as a federal matter because trains run across state lines; the CRS summary notes courts have generally found state obstructed-crossing laws preempted by federal law [S2]. A patchwork of state time limits could disrupt freight schedules and force trains to stop or hold short of towns.

A stopped train cannot always be moved quickly: a blocked crossing may reflect congestion elsewhere on the line, and a strict time limit might simply relocate the blockage to the next crossing down the line rather than eliminate it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but local: cleared crossings save drivers minutes and can save lives when emergency vehicles are involved, and the bill restores towns' power to act. The cost falls on railroads' operations and schedules, and critics argue federal uniformity serves interstate commerce. The bill never got far enough for that tradeoff to be argued on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2024, sent to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its railroads subcommittee, and the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Warren Davidson (R-OH) introduced the Railroad Responsibility Act of 2024 on August 2, 2024 [S1].
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill had zero cosponsors [S4], and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill under the rule that unpassed bills expire when a Congress ends.
Because of continued federal preemption — which the CRS summary notes courts have applied to strike down state obstructed-crossing laws [S2] — state limits on blocked crossings remain unenforceable.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest freight railroads come out ahead: no state-by-state limits on blocked crossings were created, and the court rulings that make state crossing laws unenforceable continue to stand. Drivers and towns near crossings are where they were before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Freight railroads; state crossing limits stay unenforceable

for.name: Rep. Warren Davidson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 2, 2024 to give states authority to limit blocked highway-rail crossings.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled action
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 2, 2024 and sent it to the railroads subcommittee; took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Class I freight railroads
against.what_they_did: Railroads have consistently opposed and litigated against state blocked-crossing limits, relying on federal preemption, and state laws on obstructed crossings have been struck down as preempted.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the only partisan signal is that the lone sponsor was a Republican and no cosponsors of either party joined.

industries.note: The bill would let states cap how long trains can block road crossings, forcing railroads to manage schedules, change crew practices, and absorb delays in towns that set strict limits. Railroads have long relied on federal preemption to keep state crossing rules unenforceable, so this bill targeted the legal shield protecting their operating freedom.
